articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias: More than 850,000 households without power in Alabama, Florida and Georgia
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias: More than 850,000 households without power in Alabama, Florida and Georgia
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias leaves hundreds of thousands of people without power in Alabama, Georgia and Florida, with all three states declaring emergencies
Flooding is a continuing risk, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis says as he warns of a "very hazardous situation"
Winds peaked at 120mph (193km/h) before Isaias made landfall in Florida late on Friday - images show houses battered by winds and felled trees
Two people are dead in Alabama , according to the governor, while one person was killed after a tree fell on a house in Florida , officials say
Isaias peaked as a category three hurricane , bringing heavy rain and powerful wind, but has since been downgraded
In addition to Isaias, Tropical Storm Rachel is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday, and Hurricane Simon will hit the Pacific coast of Mexico on Sunday
The city of Charleston, in South Carolina, has asked people to stay at home tonight, with high tide expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m) and "heavy rain" still possible.
"After dark, floodwater is much harder to see, and itâs impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city warns in a post on Facebook.
It also urges people not to push water into people's homes by driving down flooded streets.
There were 21 road closures during the previous high tide this morning, it says.
Ahead of the storm, Charleston warned that people would "still feel" the hurricane, despite it being "hundreds of miles away".
In an update on X, the Florida National Guard has shared pictures of troops pulling people to safety after a truck became submerged in a flooded ditch.
"Saving lives!" the post says, explaining that the soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety".
The troops were en route from Tallahassee, it adds.
The National Guard has been out supporting efforts more widely in the state. Earlier pictures show troops clearing a road of fallen trees.
Florida resident William Sexton
As Isaias hit Florida, hundreds of thousands were left without power, with trees down and houses damaged.
But for some, the storm was not as bad as they had expected.
"I'm very glad actually that it didn't go and wipe everybody's businesses and all the stuff that everybody's been working for their whole life," William Sexton, a resident of Destin in Florida, tells Reuters news agency.
"It's really expensive over here in Destin, so a lot of damage can cause a lot of money."
Sexton adds that many members of the community are older people who "have been paying and working their whole life".
Al Iannaccone also lives in Destin, Florida
Al Iannaccone, another Destin resident, also tells Reuters: "Very lucky, very lucky for as big of a hurricane as they predicted. Things were not as bad as they could be.
"Few trees down, the electricity went out probably about eight o'clock last night. So not as bad as it could be; we feel very fortunate."
We can bring you more now from Alabama Governor Kay Ivey, who has just said two people were killed in her state due to Isaias.
In a social media post, she says the storm brought heavy winds to Alabama, bringing down trees, cutting power and causing some damage.
She has also rescinded the mandatory evacuation of non-residents.
All major roads including the Intracoastal Waterway have reopened, the governor announced, although some roads remain closed.
"Fellow Alabamians, please continue being smart today as cleanup continues," she says.
Alabama Governor Kay Ivey has said two people from the state have been killed as Isais hit the south-eastern US.
"Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Ivey says in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths.
Earlier, we reported that one person had died in the state after a tree fell on a house . Another person was also killed in Florida.
Isaias is one of three storms threatening the North American continent this weekend - communities are also bracing for Tropical Storm Rachel and Hurricane Simon.
Rachel is expected to bring extreme conditions to Baja California tonight, the Mexican state which borders California. Its effects could also be felt in southern California.
NHC is warning of "damaging wind gusts" and "significant flash and urban flooding" in some areas, as well as "life-threatening surf and rip current conditions".
Meanwhile, Simon is likely to bring "catastrophic wind" and "life-threatening storm surge impacts" to the west-central coast of Mexico.
NHC has warned of heavy rainfall and "life-threatening flooding and mudslides" in the south-west. Dangerous surf and rip currents could also impact some areas.
We can now bring you the latest images out of Florida, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall there on Friday night.
The state continues to face a risk of flooding, but earlier Governor Ron DeSantis said the "water levels across Florida's Gulf Coast are expected to "continue receding throughout the day".
A boat rests on dry land in Fort Walton Beach, Florida
Damaged storefront signage is seen in Gulf Breeze, Florida
High winds caused by Isaias caused damage to trees, like the above in Destin, Florida
Flooding was felt in Tiger Point, Florida, with flood warnings still in place
In a dashboard-camera video clip released by the sheriffâs office, a tree can be seen falling on a vehicle
In Alabama, a Dale County sheriff's deputy was injured when a tree fell on him, Sheriff Mason Bynum tells Live 5 WCSC , external .
In a phone interview, Bynum says the deputy was responding to a rollover crash when a tree fell on one of the vehicles involved, trapping the driver and striking the deputy.
The driver was unharmed, but the deputy was taken to a local hospital with minor injuries, Bynum says.
In a social media post published about an hour ago , external , the Dale County Sheriffâs Office says the deputy is now back home with his family.
Meanwhile, the office is continuing to respond to reports of trees down across roads and power cuts in the county.
A tree rests in a power line in Fort Walton Beach, Florida
We have been monitoring power cuts over the past few hours, as Isaias continues to cause disruption.
The total number of outages in the three worst-hit states is moving quickly, but has dropped to just under 840,000 based on poweroutage.com reports. It was earlier at more than 850,000.
Florida, where the hurricane made landfall yesterday, currently has over 438,000 customers without power, according to the site.
Governor Ron DeSantis said earlier that more than 80% were without power in some counties in the state. Workers carrying out repairs began work last night, he added.
More than 251,000 are without power in Alabama, according to the same monitoring site.
Alabama Power, which serves 1.6 million customers, says heavy rain and strong winds have created "challenging conditions for restoration".
Poweroutage.com says just over 91,000 customers are without power in Georgia.
Georgia Power, which serves 2.8 million customers, says crews are "out where it is safe working to assess damage and restore power".
Despite Isaias not directly passing through the state, there are now more than 12,400 households without power, poweroutage.com states.
North Carolina now has more than 12,400 households without power, according to poweroutage.com.
While Isaias isn't expected to cross into the state, the US National Hurricane Center earlier warned that heavy rain could be expected in its coastal areas, with the possibility of flooding.
Isaias is still slowing down travel around Florida, Alabama, Louisiana and Georgia on Saturday.
Several airports are feeling the effects. Florida's Pensacola International Airport, which closed on Friday due to the storm, remains closed to commercial traffic, as authorities work on damage assessment. Alabama's Gulf Shores International reopened on Saturday morning following a storm-safety assessment.

There was ‌no immediate claim of responsibility, but the attack comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by the Iran-aligned Houthis
Several people were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh on Saturday that forced a suspension of operations, the country’s civil aviation authority said.
There was ‌no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, but it comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis against Saudi Arabia.
The airport had already been struck in two earlier attacks this week that left four people dead and exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s ability to defend itself as it wages war on the Houthis. Saudi Arabia’s early warning system did not issue an alert ahead of Saturday’s incident.

articles.title_zh: Trump fumes at ‘stain’ on Norway after missing out on Nobel Peace Prize
articles.content_orig:
The US president lashed out after former UN official Navi Pillay was awarded the prize, claiming the decision discredited Norway
“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t,” Trump told supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York. He added that the snub was “just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country”.
Trump called Pillay a “mystery person” and “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of” during ‌the campaign rally. “I never heard of the person. Nobody did … I know a lot of people. I’ve never heard of this particular person. But congratulations anyway.”

articles.title_zh: Simon strengthens into a Category 4 hurricane as it approaches Mexico's coast
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Hurricane Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 system as it barrels toward Mexico 's Pacific coast.
Early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said Simon’s maximum sustained winds increased to 140 mph (225 kph). A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane. Simon could bring as much as 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas receiving up to 30 inches.
The forecast was upgraded as Simon approached Mexico's southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, one of the country's most popular tourist regions.
"Simon could deliver the most significant hurricane impact to this stretch of the Mexican Pacific coast since Lidia in 2023, which damaged thousands of homes and devastated crops along the Jalisco coast," said Tyler Roys, a senior meteorologist at AccuWeather .
At the very least, Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along Jalisco’s coast and in parts of Michoacan , Colima, and Nayarit.
On Friday, forecasters warned that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with isolated rainfall totals reaching 30 inches (762 mm).
Simon is expected to make landfall on Sunday between Manzanillo — Mexico’s largest port and the main gateway for trade with Asia — and Puerto Vallarta, a popular beach destination and home to nearly 300,000 residents.
Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones by Friday afternoon.
In Manzanillo, fishermen were hauling their boats off the beach and authorities were putting up black flags along the coast to signal the beach was closed.
The Mexican Navy activated emergency response personnel in Colima and restricted maritime traffic along parts of the Pacific coast, closing ports to smaller vessels and barring larger vessels from operating in Michoacan.
Last week, Hurricane Polo made landfall on the Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, toppling trees and utility poles, flooding streets and causing other property damage.

articles.title_orig: SLCo SAR rescues China Wall hiker with leg injury
articles.title_zh: SLCo SAR rescues China Wall hiker with leg injury
articles.content_orig:
LITTLE COTTONWOOD CANYON, Oct. 10, 2026 (Gephardt Daily) — Salt Lake County Search and Rescue crews were dispatched to a Little Cottonwood Canyon area near China Wall Friday after a hiker fell while navigating a boulder field.
The fall was only about 10 feet, but left the hiker with a serious lower leg injury, and unable to stand or get back to the road.
SAR was dispatched to the scene at about 3:26 p.m. Friday. Unified Fire Authority was first on scene, and provided medical assistance to stabilized the patient’s knee.
An initial SAR team was dispatched with a litter and assisted UFA in packaging the patient for extraction.
Meanwhile, a second team was sent to assess the terrain and plan an exit route. Two additional teams followed to provide support for the ensuing carry-out.
Salt Lake County Sheriff photo
SAR and UFA worked together to carry the patient across the boulder field, down the trail, through the creek, and back to the road.
Salt Lake County Sheriff photo
There, a family member was waiting to drive them to the hospital for further evaluation.
All teams were off the mountain by 5:42 p.m.All teams were off the mountain by 5:42 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Texas Rare Earths Could Challenge China And Bring Billions To Schools
articles.title_zh: Texas Rare Earths Could Challenge China And Bring Billions To Schools
articles.content_orig:
Texas could turn a West Texas rare earth deposit into a major source of school funding while reducing America’s reliance on China for critical minerals, Texas Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham (R) said on Let’s Talk Local .
Round Top Mountain in Hudspeth County sits on state-owned land. Its development could connect two priorities Buckingham outlined in her interview with host Sarah Zubiate Bennett: securing essential materials at home and putting Texas resources to work for public education.
China accounted for 91% of global refining output for magnet rare earths in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency. That figure concerns processing, rather than ownership of all rare earth deposits.
“Well, your cell phones need rare earth minerals to work and jets require tons of them to fly,” Buckingham said in the interview.
Buckingham described domestic production as a national security priority and said she pushed prospective developers to compete rather than take the minerals to China for processing.
USA Rare Earth targets late 2028 for commercial production at Round Top. The company identifies processing facilities in Colorado and its magnet manufacturing facility in Stillwater, Oklahoma.
Bonus payments and royalties from the state’s Round Top lease go to the Permanent School Fund, which supports K-12 public education, according to the General Land Office.
“We think it’ll be tens of billions of dollars,” Buckingham said when asked about potential school-fund revenue. She also estimated the deposit could supply minerals for about 100 years.
As previously reported by The Dallas Express, Buckingham has linked revenue from state resources to public school funding and the burden on property owners.
The conversation also explores why she wants Texas to retain its land and how development could reshape the surrounding community.
Watch here for Buckingham’s explanation of the Round Top opportunity and what it could mean for Texas schools and American independence from China.
Provided by Dallas Express

articles.title_orig: Deadly Isaias weakens, rain and flooding remain a threat as storm moves across the Southeast
articles.title_zh: Deadly Isaias weakens, rain and flooding remain a threat as storm moves across the Southeast
articles.content_orig:
Robbie Berg, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Hurricane Center in Miami, told the Associated Press that while storm surge warnings have been discontinued, high wind remains a threat for the Southeast.
"So even though it has become post-tropical, it still does remain a wind threat, as well as a heavy rainfall threat. We could see some areas of significant flash flooding over the next couple of days," Berg said.
Isaias weakened quickly after making landfall on the U.S. Gulf Coast near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane Friday evening. Its powerful winds left hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle without power early Saturday.
A person has been killed in the Huffman area of Birmingham, Alabama, after a tree fell on their house, according to the Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency.
Several homes have been damaged by falling trees in the Birmingham area, officials said, but they were not aware of any other casualties.
"Power outages, downed trees, and debris remain the primary concerns across the county," the emergenct management agency said. "Crews and first responders are working hard to clear debris and restore power throughout the county."
The death is at least the second associated with Hurricane Isaias. A woman in Escambia County, Florida, in the Panhandle, died when a tree fell on her home.
Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves said on his Facebook page that the airport "took some damage." Some power was out downtown, he said, and there were trees and power lines down in some areas.
Meanwhile, strong winds blew the roof off a hotel in the city.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned that while the eye of Isaias has long passed the state, the threat of the storm is far from over.
He said Saturday in a presser that rain and flooding are still on the horizon for communities in the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend this weekend.
"The risk of flooding is still high," DeSantis said. "Sometimes these things happen a day or two days after the storm goes through. So the flooding story is not over."
DeSantis said the focus now is restoration of power. There are nearly 440,000 customers without electricity in Florida, as of 9 a.m., according to PowerOutage.com."
"Thousands of linemen and utility crews have convoyed from San Destin and along the I-10 corridor to get to work, focusing on outages in the hardest-hit communities," he said, adding: "The storm has passed. It was safe enough to go out, and they were doing it."
At least one fatality has been confirmed in the Florida Panhandle after the storm.
Escambia Sheriff Chip Simmons said on social media on Saturday that a woman died after a tree fell on a house during the storm.
"Our thoughts and prayers are obviously with that family," he said. "We will continue to be out there in full force."
The number of customers left without power in the Southeast continues to climb as a weakened Isaias makes its way across the region. More than 884,000 customers are without power on Saturday morning, according to the latest data.
Here's the latest breakdown by state, according to PowerOutage.com :
While Isaias has weakened significantly since it made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane on Friday night, what remains of the storm still packs a punch.
CBS Meteorologist Rob Marciano said the winds are still about 35 mph, with higher wind gusts.
Here is a look at the strongest winds recorded as of Friday.
More than 860,000 customers are without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, as of 7:30 a.m. Saturday.
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey said Saturday morning that her team is worried about "strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes" as Isaias continues to move across the state.
She urged people to have "reliable information" as conditions develop.
"We often hear in emergency management: Hope for the best. Prepare for the worst," she said . "That is the approach we need with this particular storm system. After all, we only want to see one Tide roll this weekend. Y'all be safe, heed local warnings and stay weather aware."
Isaias, now a post-tropical cyclone, continues to weaken as it moves further inland across Alabama. It is forecast to enter the Tennessee Valley later Saturday and into Sunday, the National Hurricane Center said in its final advisory at 5 a.m. ET.
The storm is moving at 14 mph with maximum sustained winds near 35 mph and higher gusts. Forecasters said it will continue to slowly weaken as the day goes and is expected to dissipate on Sunday.
However, rain and flooding are still a threat. Through the weekend, Isaias is expected to produce up to 8 inches of rainfall across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia, the center said. Localized totals up to 15 inches are possible.
Across much of the remainder of the Southeast, rainfall up to 5 inches is expected, while localized higher amounts up to 10 inches are possible, especially across the Southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.
"Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region," the center said.
A risk for tornadoes will persist Saturday morning through the afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.
Hurricane Simon strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm as it barrels toward Mexico's Pacific coast.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said early Saturday Simon's maximum sustained winds increased to 145 mph. Simon could bring as much as 10 to 20 inches of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas receiving up to 30 inches, the center said.
The bulletin also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare, saying the hurricane will make landfall late Saturday or early Sunday, but tropical storm-strength winds could arrive much sooner.
Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along Jalisco's coast and in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Nayarit.
"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the NHC said.
The Trump administration approved federal emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama on Friday night.
This would allow the Federal Emergency Management Agency to offer federal disaster assistance to supplement state, tribal and local response efforts for emergency conditions caused by the storm.
In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties ahead of the storm's landfall. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey, who told tourists and visitors in the state's coastal areas to leave immediately, issued a state of emergency for 40 counties.
"This emergency declaration will help cut tape for our federal partners to aid in any response. We will continue to stay engaged with the Trump Administration and other partners as we brace for this storm. Fellow Alabamians, y'all stay weather aware," Ivey said in a statement.
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also declared a state of emergency.
"(The Department of Homeland Security) and FEMA stand ready to support DeSantis and Ivey as they lead efforts to protect lives and communities," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X.
Hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama, Georgia and the Florida Panhandle were without power early Saturday after Isaias hit the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane and left flooded roads and downed trees in its wake as it moved inland.
According to poweroutage.us, as of 5 a.m., 834,061 customers have lost power.
Florida — with 436,443 — has the most customers without power. Alabama has 314,540 customers and Georgia has 83,078 without electricity.
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, told the Associated Press that the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator.
"As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate," Mowry added.

articles.title_orig: Joel Oxley Goes Out on ’TOP
articles.title_zh: Joel Oxley Goes Out on ’TOP
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › News Makers
Hubbard Radio’s WTOP(FM) has been one of the top revenue-generating stations in the United States for more than a decade, according to BIA estimates. Although it is in Nielsen Market No. 8, it regularly beats out stations in the larger markets to pull off that feat.
WTOP’s over-the-air revenue in 2023, the most recent for which BIA published estimates, was $66.3 million. WTOP led the BIA list 13 times over the previous 14 years. It also pulls in consistently high ratings.
That remarkable streak occurred under the leadership of Joel Oxley, president/GM of WTOP, WFED(AM), the Federal News Network and the 2060 Digital Washington platform.
Oxley, who is about to retire, has been named to receive the 2026 NAB National Radio Award from the National Association of Broadcasters .
We asked him about the uniqueness of the Washington market, changes in newsroom workflows and his secret to generating revenue. Text has been edited for length and clarity.
Radio World: Are you optimistic about the radio broadcast business model going forward?
Joel Oxley: Yes, I think it can still work, but I think you’ve got to have great products, and you must have products that connect to people. You’ve also got to understand that radio is great distribution still. But you’ve got to be playing in all the platforms. As long as you do that, radio can be still a great part of the business.
But it’s not the 1990s anymore. You’ve got to be looking at the business model differently. You can’t be sitting around waiting for agency avails — I mean it’s great when you get agency avails, we love agencies when they call us and give us a bit of business. [But] you have to be incredibly proactive and make sure that you’re getting out and figuring out what you can do to help solve your clients’ needs.
Find solutions. It could be digital. It might not be over the air radio every time.
RW: Does AM have a future as the margins continue to shrink?
Oxley: That’s really going to be market-dependent, signal-dependent. It’s getting harder. I don’t think anybody would tell you that it’s an easy business. We have found some good uses for our AMs, and I think others can too.
Especially when AMs are paired with translators, especially smaller markets, they make a whole hell of a lot of sense.
We’ve experimented with AM digital. There are ways to make AM sound better. There can still be a place for it. But I’m not going to tell you that it’s an easy business.
RW: What makes the Washington radio market unique?
Oxley: I tell people: It’s always a good thing to be in the all-news business in the news capital of the world.
The market has really grown, too. It wasn’t that long ago, honestly, that it was a 2-million-person market. Now it’s over 6 million. If you throw in Baltimore, it’s like 9.
Also the growth of the federal government has meant a lot more jobs have come here. All kinds of government contractors. That’s what makes us unique.
Unlike most markets, there’s also a lot of political influence advertising here, and that’s a great advertising category for us. There’s more issue money spent here than anywhere.
Advocacy money used to be really big for us, but it’s a smaller part of what we do now.
However, the government contracting side has grown a ton, and we see that as an area that’s going to continue to grow.
RW: Many radio companies are downsizing their physical footprint. You opened a large new facility seven years ago. Do you still need that much space now?
Oxley: No, we don’t. The reality is a lot more people work remotely now.
The tools are so much better. Our reporters, a lot of them do amazing things with just an iPhone with audio and video.
Our remote work has increased significantly. The workflows have changed. Salespeople can work from anywhere. Docking stations and good connectivity means that you can do your job from all over the place with a laptop, let alone your phone.
So if I had it to do over again, we wouldn’t need anywhere near as much space as we have.
RW: How is AI changing how work gets done in the WTOP newsroom?
Oxley: Lots of ways. But we’re being trying to be very careful and thoughtful about it. Certainly, being in the news business, we cannot afford mistakes. We can’t afford misinformation.
We insist that everything that we do has a pair of human eyes on it, and that people are reading it through, proofreading, fact-checking. We’ve got to make sure things are right. If you lose your credibility, you’ve lost.
RW: Do you worry about the future of all-news radio given the massive amount of instantly available information that Americans now have right on their phone?
Oxley: Sure. You’ve got to always be concerned about that. But we’re on the phone, too, for people to consume our products.
RW: There is great pressure to compete with digital platforms. You’ve gone through the digital transition. How do you choose which ones are successful without diluting the original value of the radio broadcast business?
Oxley: It’s a point a lot of people miss. It’s great to go into all kinds of different platforms and all kinds of different things, but you got to make sure you get ROI. You’ve got to make sure that there is a business plan. You can’t just go into it without making sure that you’re also supporting that with advertising.
I think that’s a missing piece for a lot of folks. They go into it and they’re getting tons of hits or tons of views, but they don’t do much because you can’t monetize.
RW: The Federal News Network airs on WFED(AM), which isn’t a highly rated station. Why is the network successful?
Oxley: So it’s not a ratings play. It’s about reaching the right people. It’s reaching government decisionmakers. CIOs for example, really high up in the government levels.
And while we really don’t see that necessarily in the ratings, we do see it in our streaming numbers and our podcast numbers, where we see the number of people who are consuming that product. It goes pretty deep.
These are things that really matter to the upper levels of government, and we know that we’re getting pretty good numbers there. But it’s a niche play for sure.
Sometimes it’s about getting the right thousand people. Sometimes about getting the right six people. Sometimes it’s about getting the right two people. So it’s a different play than broadcast in a sense, but it’s been going really well for us.
RW: You’ve supported the work done by Dave Kolesar with AM HD Radio at WSHE Frederick, Md., formerly WWFD. It’s a full digital-only station. What does the future look like for full-time digital AM and for that station specifically?
Oxley: I’ll tell you, it sounds so much better. I think that it’s something that if you can find the right format, it’s going to be a much better play than trying to just go with traditional AM. I don’t know that it’s necessarily been proven yet, that somebody can make a business out of that.
I still think it’s a viable way to go because it does make me forget that I’m on AM. It’s like I’m listening to FM.
RW: You play music but no commercials on that station. How long can that go on for?
Oxley: It’s more of a public service play right now. It’s more experimental. No, it’s not making a profit.

articles.title_orig: Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat
Nine people, including children, died in a mass murder on Friday in Erie, Pennsylvania , after a gun-wielding attacker opened fire outside a home and then entered the property, according to authorities.
The suspected attacker was also found dead as police responded to the deadly violence, which triggered a standoff involving Erie police officers and tactical teams.
Police discovered the killings at about 5pm when officers were called to a residence following reports of gunfire. Witnesses told authorities that they had seen an attacker with a gun outside the property before making his way inside.
Responding officers discovered two women lying dead in the street, both having suffered fatal gunshot wounds.
The situation quickly developed into a standoff as police officers and tactical personnel surrounded the residence. More gunshots were heard coming from inside the home, and officers entered the place.
Inside, police said they made a devastating discovery, finding seven additional victims, including children, along with the suspected attacker. Investigators believe the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Erie’s police chief, Rick Lorah, spoke about the scale of the mass murder, describing the scene as among the most distressing and heartbreaking he had witnessed.
“The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said. “At this time, we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public.”
He added: “Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.”
Authorities on Saturday said they were still investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings, with authorities attempting to determine a motive for the violence.
The city of Erie also issued a statement on social media confirming that the suspected shooter had died and that the immediate danger had passed.
The statement described the case as a “terrible tragedy”, although the city’s statement did not provide further information about the events leading up to the shooting.
after newsletter promotion
“We understand that the news brings deep shock and sorrow to our residents, and we want to assure the public that the situation has been contained,” the city said.
Figures from the Gun Violence Archive indicate that the killings in Erie marked at least the 19th mass murder of the year. Such cases are defined as ones in which four or more victims are murdered.
Many of those mass murders have been what are considered family annihilations , in which an attacker kills multiple close family members.
The nonpartisan archive also indicated that the killings in Erie were among more than 500 mass shootings across the US since the beginning of January. Mass shootings are defined as cases in which four or more victims are shot whether fatally or non-fatally.
Mass shootings for years have remained a persistent problem in the US, often intensifying public demands for stronger gun control measures at the federal level.
Despite those calls, Congress has not enacted such restrictions sought over the years.

articles.title_orig: Indian police crack down on 'Cockroach' protest in Delhi
articles.title_zh: Indian police crack down on 'Cockroach' protest in Delhi
articles.content_orig:
Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:
Videos released by opposition leaders show that several senior figures were detained in New Delhi on Saturday.
They include Arvind Kejriwal, leader of the Aam Aadmi Party and former chief minister of Delhi .
"It's official... we are living under an absolute dictatorship," Kejriwal wrote on X.
Mamata Banerjee, who lost power as West Bengal's chief minister earlier this year, was also detained.
Pinarayi Vijayan, a communist leader who headed the southern state of Kerala until May, was among those detained.
Rahul Gandhi, leader of India's opposition Congress party , called the crackdown an act of "cowardice" and described Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah, right-wing, Hindu nationalist RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and National Security Adviser Ajit Doval as "the villains of this story" who were "slowly finding the space closing around them. We are closing that space."
Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Rahul Gandhi's sister and a Congress MP, wrote in a social media post: "India is not a democracy anymore. It is a dictatorship being run by Mr. Narendra Modi and Mr. Amit Shah."
Opposition parties and critics have warned that the electoral-roll revision exercise could strip millions of people of their voting rights and give an advantage to Prime Minister Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission of India has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, saying the "special intensive revision" aims to remove duplicate and ineligible voters.
The protests echo the CJP's mass mobilization in July, which forced the then education minister to resign over an examination scandal.
This time, demonstrators are demanding the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.
Tens of thousands of security personnel have been deployed and roads barricaded across New Delhi to prevent the latest Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstration.
Police have detained thousands of protesters in a major crackdown. Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital.
Some protesters who turned back from Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site, have been waiting in different parts of central Delhi, determined to hold their ground.
The CJP has urged people who believe they or someone they know has been unlawfully detained to fill out an online form as soon as possible, saying it is collecting information to support affected volunteers and other individuals.
The protest targeted Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over voter list revisions that critics say favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP.
If you're joining us now, here's a helpful reminder about why India's youth are rising up this time.
DW Hindi's Adarsh Sharma, who is on the ground in New Delhi, spoke to protesters as they faced a security crackdown.
He caught up with one protester who managed to avoid detention.
"We were running back and forth. When the police are moving forward, we go back. When they are withdrawing, we are moving forward," the protester told DW.
The protester described the heavy police presence as a "game of perception."
"Where you have 20 protesters and 10 media persons, there are 100 police personnel standing. It seems like a joke, what they are doing with taxpayers' money," the protester said.
Another protester, Jasmine, described how the morning unfolded for the demonstrators.
"We have been playing a game of cat and mouse with the police, trying to stop them from picking us up," she said.
"I don't think we have ever seen something like this happening. Protesting is a fundamental right… it's such a convoluted idea to take permission to protest… you are protesting against a government, will you ask permission from the same government? They are not going to give it," she said.
Ajinkya Shinde, who was handed the responsibility of leading the Cockroach Janta Party's protest following the detentions of its main leaders, has made his first statement — calling for a continued march to Jantar Mantar.
"We appeal to everyone to march towards Jantar Mantar! If Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar," he said in a video post made by the CJP on X.
Indian media outlets, including Scroll and Newslaundry, reported that their journalists had been detained by police while covering the 'Cockroach' party protest. The journalists were later released.
Newslaundry reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports said journalists were physically assaulted.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an independent nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom and defends journalists' rights worldwide, has called on Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers.
It has also urged police to return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in New Delhi and the police response without interference.
In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), India ranked 157th out of 180 countries, down six places from 2025. Press freedom groups have raised concerns about the use of criminal laws against journalists and the impact of such measures on independent journalism.
Detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother is reported to have died on Saturday.
Indian media reports said that Dipke's paternal grandmother had been suffering from a prolonged illness and had been unwell in recent days. She died in her native village in Maharashtra, reports said.
News agency ANI, citing police sources, reported that the Delhi Police had informed Dipke of his grandmother's death. It was now up to the CJP leader to decide whether to continue his protest while under detention or travel back for the funeral rites.
Dipke was detained aboard his plane after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday morning, ahead of the protest. He was traveling from Mumbai.
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has indicated that it will press on with its protest despite its leaders and supporters being detained.
CJP's National Organization In-Charge Ajinkya Shinde will lead the protest at Jantar Mantar until Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remain in detention, the group said in a statement on X.
The CJP also shared a video of Dipke purportedly recorded on Friday night, anticipating a potential detention.
"If you are seeing this video, it means Ashutosh, Saurav and I have been arrested," Dipke says in the video.
"After us, Ajinkya will lead this movement," he says.
In a separate post, the CJP alleged that its three detained leaders had been taken to an undisclosed location, were being denied access to lawyers and had been cut off from "all contact with others."
The formal association of advocates at India's apex court called for urgent intervention by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant after several lawyers were detained by Delhi police.
This comes amid a reported crackdown on protesters attempting to reach the national capital, specifically central Delhi, to protest against India's chief election commissioner over alleged misconduct.
The arrested lawyers include those protesting outside the premises of the Supreme Court of India, as well as lawyers inside their chambers, legal news website, Bar and Bench, reported.
The Supreme Court Bar Association passed a resolution condemning the use of "excessive force against, and detention of, senior and young advocates, particularly women advocates, who were peacefully protesting in the Supreme Court area today."
The advocates' body expressed "grave concern" and requested the CJI to take action to ensure that the "whereabouts and safety of every detained advocate are ascertained."

articles.title_orig: Different voices, shared challenges: mental health in athletics | FEATURE
articles.title_zh: Different voices, shared challenges: mental health in athletics | FEATURE
articles.content_orig:
Mental health in athletics
It was a fleeting exchange at a press conference, but it touched on a much wider issue.
Speaking at the World Athletics Relays in Gaborone earlier this year, Zaynab Dosso and Elaine Thompson-Herah were both asked about the mental side of elite sport.
Italian sprinter Dosso was clear about the importance she places on it. “It’s very important to speak about mental health,” said the world indoor 60m champion. “You can train however many hours you want, but if your head doesn’t follow then you’re not going to get anywhere.
“Last September I started working with a psychologist. Every single athlete should take care of their mental health because it’s just as important as their physical health.”
The same question was then put to Thompson-Herah. “Coming back from injury has been challenging, mentally and physically,” said the five-time Olympic champion.
“But I’m a tough cookie. I’ve never been to therapy, I don’t believe in it. I’m my own therapy. I do believe in God, though. I also have a supportive team who believes in me, and I believe in myself.”
The contrast was striking. Both athletes acknowledged the mental challenges of elite sport, yet they had very different ideas about how to deal with them.
Across a sport spanning more than 200 countries, there are inevitably huge differences in the way mental health is understood, discussed and treated. Professional psychological support may be commonplace for some athletes. Others may turn first to family, friends, teammates or coaches. Elsewhere, stigma, lack of awareness or limited access to services can make the route to support far less straightforward.
US 800m runner Juliette Whittaker has spoken with remarkable openness about her own experience. During her time at Stanford University, Whittaker won two individual NCAA titles before qualifying for the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. Her results suggested a young athlete whose career was progressing almost perfectly.
Juliette Whittaker in action at the US Olympic Trials (© Getty Images)
The reality was very different. She later described it as the “hardest, saddest and loneliest” year of her life.
After winning her first NCAA title, the happiness had disappeared by the following day. After the second, it lasted less than an hour. Whittaker responded by setting herself another target, believing that perhaps reaching the Olympics would finally make her feel differently. It didn’t.
“I truly believed that if I ran well enough, achieved enough, proved myself enough, I would finally feel enough,” she said.
Instead, her sense of self-worth became increasingly tied to her performances. When running stopped providing the fulfilment she expected from it, she struggled to know where else to find it. After returning from Paris, her mental health deteriorated further. Feelings of emptiness became guilt and shame, and she stopped telling people how badly she was struggling.
In May 2025, Whittaker attempted to take her own life.
Friends found her and took her to hospital. She spent a week in a psychiatric unit and later attended group therapy three days a week, while also taking the longest break from running she had ever had.
Whittaker credits the people around her with playing a huge part in her recovery. “At a time when I had completely given up on myself, I had villages of people who refused to give up on me,” she said, speaking at Stanford’s GameFaces event earlier this year.
“One year ago, I was in a hospital bed with absolutely no desire to live,” she added. “Today I’m standing in front of you.”
Her experience also changed the way she viewed athletics. “Running is a huge part of my life,” she said. “But it is not all of me. It is not the source of my worth.”
After spending so long keeping her feelings to herself, she had learned another lesson: “Asking for help is one of the bravest things you can do.” But asking for help assumes an athlete recognises what is happening to them, feels able to talk about it and knows where to turn.
Research in recent years has examined some of those barriers in different parts of the world.
A 2025 paper on mental health among elite runners in Kenya highlighted the importance of cultural and socioeconomic context. Its authors pointed to issues including the availability, accessibility and affordability of mental-health services, and cautioned against assuming that approaches developed in wealthier countries can simply be transferred elsewhere.
A separate 2024 study involving 20 Chinese elite athletes , as well as coaches and team officials, found that cultural attitudes and sporting environments could influence whether athletes sought help. Participants spoke about issues including depressed mood, competition anxiety and sleep problems, while stigma – including fears of being regarded as weak – was among the barriers identified. Athletes were often more comfortable turning first to teammates, friends or parents than to formal mental-health services.
Kenya’s Wilfred Bungei recognises some of that from his own experience. The 2008 Olympic 800m champion has spoken openly about his problems with alcohol and mental health after his competitive career ended.
Wilfred Bungei in action at the 2008 Olympics (© Getty Images)
Among his wake-up calls were missing important engagements because he had been drinking, and realising that his children were uncomfortable being in the car with him when they knew he was drunk. Looking back 10 years or more, Bungei says alcoholism and mental-health problems in Kenya were often seen as matters of personal choice.
“People with mental-health problems were stigmatised,” he says. He believes attitudes have improved since then and there is now more empathy, although some of that stigma remains.
“The talk behind the scenes doesn’t indicate a society that has fully embraced mental-health issues,” he says. “Most people would rather suffer from the inside than be open.”
For Bungei, his family was crucial in recognising that he needed help. “Family is the first pillar,” he says. “If one’s family accepts that this person is sick and needs help, the individual wouldn’t care much about what society says because they know, ‘I have people who care’.”
He has sometimes compared alcoholism with diabetes when trying to explain to people that addiction is an illness rather than simply a personal failing. “The first thing is accept who you are and don’t care about the noise,” he says.
Bungei also believes athletes need more help preparing for life after competition. “Athletes retire early in life and they have money and plenty of free time,” he says. “Remember, athletes live a strict life 365 days a year as sportsmen and women.”
He says there is still no clear roadmap in Kenya to help athletes cope with that transition. He has, however, since found another role within the sport. Through his work with the World Athletics Media Academy, he says he has regained a sense of “purpose and responsibility” from training as a commentator.
He hopes eventually to use that platform to speak more widely about mental-health issues affecting sportsmen and women in African countries, and what could be done to support them.
Singapore’s Shanti Pereira has spoken about a different kind of mental struggle during the years between her early breakthrough and her rise to the top of Asian sprinting.
Sprinter Shanti Pereira of Singapore (© Getty Images)
After winning the SEA Games 200m title on home soil in 2015, Pereira found it difficult to deal with the expectations that followed. Results stalled, injuries followed and, in 2018, she lost both her Sport Excellence Scholarship and her university scholarship within the space of a week.
Speaking to CNA in 2022, she said that physically she still felt capable of running personal and national records, “but mentally I wasn’t there”.
“There was a lot of self-doubt that kind of grew as the years went by,” she said. At times she lost her motivation and became afraid of performing badly

articles.title_orig: When could Zverev reach World No. 1 for the first time?
articles.title_zh: When could Zverev reach World No. 1 for the first time?
articles.content_orig:
When can Alexander Zverev climb to the No. 1 spot in the PIF ATP Rankings and become the 30th member of the prestigious ATP No. 1 Club?
Zverev currently holds 9,720 points in the PIF ATP Live Rankings, trailing current World No. 1 Jannik Sinner by 1,230 points.
With Sinner ending his 2026 season due to injury, there are two paths for the German to reach the top spot as early as 2 November.
Zverev would become the World No. 1 by winning the Rolex Shanghai Masters crown and reaching the semi-finals of the ATP 500 event in Vienna.
Alternatively, the 29-year-old would also secure the top ranking by reaching the Shanghai final and winning the title in Vienna.
Zverev first broke into the Top 10 in May 2017 and reached a career-high World No. 2 for the first in June 2022. If successful in his bid to become the World No. 1, Zverev would become only the second German player to reach the pinnacle of the PIF ATP Rankings, after Boris Becker in 1991.
A two-time Nitto ATP Finals champion, Zverev would become the newest member of the ATP No. 1 Club since Sinner in June 2024.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Tropical Storm Rachel is expected to make landfall either in northern Baja California or San Diego County as early as Saturday night, bringing with it a slew of potential hazards, including damaging coastal flooding.
The National Hurricane Center warned that Rachel,  spinning hundreds of miles off the coast of San Diego, could pick up some strength before arriving on the West Coast — an unusual occurrence for storms in the tropical eastern Pacific.
Typically, storms weaken significantly once they enter those cooler waters. But El Niño conditions and an ongoing marine heat wave have pushed ocean temperatures 10 to 13 degrees higher than normal, providing a far-more-conducive environment for Rachel.
“It’s notable that this is an unusual event that’s being made possible by both coincidence of this early arriving low-pressure trough off the coast of California and the record warm — and I do mean record warm — ocean temperatures off the coast of California right now,” UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said during a briefing  Friday.
The blistering heat that has baked Southern California for days is coming to an end, with rain on tap for the weekend and early next week, along with a risk of potentially damaging coastal flooding.
The National Weather Service office in San Diego on Friday issued a rare tropical storm watch for most of San Diego County, including San Diego, Chula Vista, Carlsbad and Oceanside, meaning that tropical storm-force winds are possible over the next 48 hours. It’s only the second time a tropical storm watch has  been issued in California.
Coastal flooding will remain the biggest concern for the region in the coming days, particularly for south-facing shores, given the combination of high tides, a higher-than-typical water level and the arriving tropical storm. Swells will not only bring the potential for water intrusion, but also hazardous surf — ranging from 3 to 6 feet in some areas — and rip currents, according to the weather service.
Officials had predicted that tides in Southern California would be 1 foot to 1.5 feet above normal what would ordinarily be expected without the abnormally warm ocean temperatures wrought by El Niño .
Around 9 a.m. Friday, the high tide in San Diego and La Jolla was coming in 17 inches higher than the official prediction, which doesn’t account for hotter-than-normal ocean waters or swells from tropical storms, according to NOAA’s tide forecasts. Tides were coming in 16 inches higher than the official prediction in Santa Monica and 14 inches higher in San Francisco as of Friday morning.
“We’ve got water that’s already high and then we’re going to have periods of high tides each morning and evening and then on top of that we have high surf,” said Miguel Miller, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in San Diego. “We have all these things stacking up on each other and we’ve already seen in recent weeks how just the high tides, even without the large surf, is putting water into places where it doesn’t usually go.”
Forecasters are warning that south-facing beaches in Southern California could be particularly at risk of flooding on account of Tropical Storm Rachel this weekend.
A coastal flood advisory for Ventura, Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties — warning of the potential for flooding in beach parking lots, boardwalks and roads, with isolated road closures expected, along with minor coastal erosion — is expected to remain in effect through Tuesday afternoon.
Coastal cities including Laguna Beach, Newport Beach and Long Beach have already seen significant flooding. Long Beach issued a mandatory evacuation order for residents of Seaside Walk between 64th and 66th Place.
While tropical moisture from the remnants of Rachel is expected to deliver only light rain to much of Southern California between Sunday morning and Monday night, the Mojave Desert, the Inland Empire and portions of San Diego County could see more significant precipitation.
The weather service is warning that there is a moderate, or 40% chance, of excessive rainfall that could lead to flash flooding in places like San Diego, El Cajon, Chula Vista, Escondido, Palm Springs and Twentynine Palms. A moderate risk means that numerous flash floods are likely, and that many streams may flood. There is a chance that the San Diego River near Fashion Valley could reach minor flood stage.
There’s also a 15% chance of that occurring in Oceanside, San Clemente, Laguna Niguel, Riverside, San Bernardino, Las Vegas and the California-Arizona border; and a 5% chance in places like Huntington Beach, Santa Ana, Long Beach, Anaheim, Pomona, Victorville, Barstow, and most of Arizona and southern Utah.
Newport Beach was one of several coastal communities to see flooding Friday as residents braced for Tropical Storm Rachel, which is expected to cause more issues over the weekend.
In Los Angeles County, rain is expected to be light to moderate, ranging from about a quarter of an inch to an inch across much of the region. A bit more rain is expected in the San Gabriel Mountains, according to the weather service office in Oxnard. Rain rates are probably going to be a quarter of an inch per hour or less, making debris flow and landslides unlikely.
A bit more rain is expected in Orange County with coastal areas receiving anywhere from half an inch to an inch over the weekend and into early next week. Coastal sections of San Diego County could see between an inch and an inch and a half of precipitation with higher rain levels predicted farther inland.
In the modern record, only two storms  have passed through the state at tropical-storm strength.
The first — nicknamed El Cordonazo, or the Lash of St. Francis — hit Long Beach and San Pedro in September 1939 . It dumped 5.62 inches of rain on L.A. over three days, spawned wind gusts of up to 65 mph and resulted in 45 deaths from flooding, with an additional 48 deaths at sea.
There was also Nora in September 1997, which was briefly at tropical storm strength as its center passed along the California-Arizona border, but California was spared the kind of damage it delivered to Baja California. Street flooding was reported in Imperial County, the Coachella Valley and San Diego, while big waves boosted by Nora and another storm sent breakers crashing into beachfront properties in Seal Beach, seriously damaging three homes and resulting in minor damage to 45 others.
Nora arrived during a “very strong” El Niño season. That pattern is linked to above-average hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific, and also is usually tied to above-average rainfall for Southern California in the winter.
That climate pattern sees the heating of ocean waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, which spur changes in the atmosphere that can affect weather around the world.
Strong surf across Southern California this weekend blasted through a seawall in Long Beach, caused a massive sinkhole at a celebrity’s Malibu home and damaged several Dana Point homes, among other issues.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center said  Thursday that there is virtually a 100% chance that the El Niño this season will be categorized as “very strong.” There’s also an 83% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest on record, which goes back to 1950, up from a 75% probability forecast last month.
“With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed,” the Climate Prediction Center said Thursday.
There have been only four “very strong” El Niños in the modern record — 1982-83, 1991-92, 1997-98 and 2015-16. Two of them — in 1982-83 and 1997-98 — deluged downtown Los Angeles with over 30 inches of rain, more than double the area’s average

China and the European Union have the potential to deepen economic and trade cooperation by addressing their differences through negotiations and providing businesses with a more stable and predictable environment, a Chinese trade expert told CGTN on Saturday, following the two sides' latest trade talks in Beijing.
The remarks followed the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, co-chaired by Chinese Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic in Beijing from Thursday to Friday. A joint statement released on Friday said the two sides had agreed to maintain stable bilateral economic and trade ties and make them more balanced.
"The statement has made it very clear that both sides agree that we are going to negotiate in a better way," said Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.
China and the EU have complementary advantages in markets, innovation and businesses, Zhou said, adding that the two sides could better address uncertainties and restrictions through dialogue.
He said policy stability and predictability were crucial to encouraging businesses to invest and expand cooperation. "When enterprises are going to make investments, they have to understand that the situation will be stable."
Supply chains and industrial chains are built on collaboration and trust, Zhou said, adding that businesses would be more willing to strengthen ties if they believed cooperation would bring them further opportunities.
The joint statement outlined 16 areas of consensus, covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform. The two sides also agreed to continue exploring the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain goods within the framework of WTO rules and reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles.
Zhou said China and the EU could help restore confidence in global trade governance amid growing uncertainty and protectionism.
China and the EU are firm supporters of globalization, he said, calling for stronger support for the multilateral trading system, including through improvements to dispute settlement and efforts to address emerging issues such as e-commerce.
The two sides also identified potential cooperation in artificial intelligence, the digital economy and new energy. Zhou said turning that potential into concrete business and investment opportunities would depend partly on whether companies had confidence in policy stability and the prospects for cooperation.
China and the EU agreed to hold their next meeting under the trade and investment consultation mechanism in March 2027, with a ministerial video conference scheduled for January. Both sides also agreed to maintain close communication and promote the early implementation of the agreed outcomes.

At 9.30am on June 16, 2022, Megan* braced herself and clicked on the Zoom link. She was about to find out whether she had the gene mutation for early onset Alzheimer’s disease . She knew the condition was in her family; she’d watched her own mother – a woman who loved to cook and dance, who changed her curtains to match the seasons – die at 65, after almost 15 awful years. “She was a husk,” says Megan. “She couldn’t speak, she weighed 40 kilograms.” Two uncles and an aunt had also died of Alzheimer’s, and her maternal grandmother. There was a 50/50 chance she had the mutation – and if she did, there was a 100 per cent chance she’d get the disease.
Megan was 55 years old at the time, with thick hair, blue eyes and unlined skin. Trained as a nurse, she was married, with three sons and an air of practical kindness: the sort of person who stops at the zebra crossing even if the pedestrian isn’t quite there yet; who says hello to everyone she sees on the street in her small home town in rural Victoria. She had no symptoms of cognitive decline, no signs of trouble at all. But a determinative mutation is like a time bomb. It will go off – the only question is when.
The genetic counsellor joined the Zoom call. At 9.35, she broke the news. Megan has the same mutation as her mother – a pathogenic variation to her Presenilin 1 gene (PSEN1). She will get Alzheimer’s disease.
Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, accounting for up to 70 per cent of cases worldwide. The rest is split between frontotemporal lobe dementia, Lewy body dementia, vascular and mixed dementias, Huntington’s and Parkinson’s disease dementia, and various dementias caused by brain injury. There are even, rarely and tragically, more than 100 genetic conditions that cause dementia in children.
Like every other form of dementia, Alzheimer’s is caused by the progressive death – often over years – of tens of billions of brain cells (at autopsy, the brain of someone with dementia may have a volume of up to 40 per cent less than that of a healthy person). It was first described in 1901, when Alois Alzheimer, a notably dedicated and meticulous German physician, took a 51-year-old woman called Auguste Deter, a seamstress, wife and mother, into his care. Alzheimer gave Deter some simple tests, including writing her own name. “Auguse”, she wrote, her pen trailing away on the “e”. “I have lost myself, so to speak,” she told him.
Over the following years, Alzheimer could do nothing to help as Deter’s condition deteriorated. But he continued caring for her for free, and when she died in 1906 he conducted her autopsy, preparing the first microscope slides ever to reveal the two “peculiar substance[s]” now known to be the twin hallmarks of Alzheimer’s: amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles.
After Megan heard the news that winter morning, she got off Zoom, left her house, and started walking. After a few minutes, a car pulled up beside her. It was her sister, Jillian, who lives in the same town, on her way home from work. Jillian was also 55 years old, with thick hair, blue eyes and unlined skin. Also a trained nurse, also a mother to three children, she is six minutes younger than Megan, and her identical twin.
Jillian leaned over, and Megan bent down to the window. “I took one look at her face,” says Jillian now, “and I knew. I went home and said to my husband, ‘I’ve got it. I’ve got it too.’ ”
Why does dementia have such a grip on the human imagination? In surveys around the world, people – especially as they reach mid-life – routinely name it as their greatest health fear: greater than heart disease, greater even than cancer. Perhaps it’s because it feels so close: as simple as blanking on a word, misplacing the remote, getting lost in a sentence – and also so inconceivably far away. In what unimaginable world could we end up oblivious to the things we love, not knowing our own names, no longer recognising the faces of our children? Dementia, above all, is a disease of loss: how could we bear to know such losses are coming?
This is exactly what Megan and Jillian are facing. Jillian’s own genetic counselling appointment was at noon on the same day as her sister’s. At 12.01, she confirmed she, too, had the PSEN1 mutation. Alzheimer’s was coming for her, too.
The next few months were horrendous for both women. “I started walking in the dark,” says Megan. “Walking down dark laneways, hoping I would come across someone in a bad mood.” “And I just cried,” says Jillian. “Shane [her husband] and I just cried and cried for weeks.”
Things are much better now – of which more later – but, as Jillian puts it, they’re always wondering if this might be the day Alzheimer’s symptoms begin. “You forget to do something, you do something stupid, and you go, ‘Is this it?’ ” she says. “I’ll say to Shane, ‘Is that it starting already?’ ”
No wonder she’s worried. Last year, for the first time ever, dementia became the biggest cause of death in Australia: a 39 per cent rise in the past decade alone. Ninety thousand new dementia cases are now being diagnosed each year, and one in 12 Australians are either living with it, or looking after someone who is. As other fatal diseases – cancer, heart disease – have become increasingly treatable, dementia has not. Despite millions of research hours and billions of research dollars, there is still no cure. Just as it was 120 years go, dementia today is a death sentence.
But now, finally, things are changing. In the past 12 months, two breakthrough new drugs have been approved, a new diagnostic blood test has become available, and new research about prevention and rehabilitation has been published. And so, for the first time in history, we can legitimately ask: can the future of dementia be different from the past?
We’ve known for more than a generation that most dementia is caused by the mis-formation of proteins in the brain. These proteins – different in different forms of dementia – are all present in healthy brains, but in dementia they go rogue, destroying neuronal function. This process can begin years – even decades – before symptoms are evident. But eventually, as it progresses, the most fundamental processes of life – heartbeat, breathing, swallowing – are compromised. Most people with dementia die of aspiration pneumonia, when food is accidentally sucked into the lungs.
What we haven’t known until recently, however, is that almost half of all cases are preventable – or at least delayable. Contrary to popular myth, less than one per cent of all dementia is inevitable, caused by determinative – 100 per cent guaranteed – gene variants like Megan’s and Jillian’s. Even “risk” genes, like the APOE4 gene variant Chris Hemsworth carries , only increase your susceptibility; they don’t cause disease outright. So for many of us, dementia is, to a greater or lesser extent, avoidable. And in July, the World Health Organisation updated its official dementia guidelines to reflect this fact, stating that “up to 45 per cent of the risks can be attributed to modifiable risk factors such as tobacco, alcohol use, social isolation, physical inactivity, air pollution and noncommunicable diseases, including high blood pressure and diabetes.”
Many healthy people do get dementia; many risks are beyond our control. But if possible, why not try to modify the ones we can?
Kaarin Anstey is the director of the UNSW Ageing Futures Institute. She studies non-pharmacological interventions for dementia. Drilling down on the WHO risk factors, she explains that type 2 diabetes “increases the risk of dementia by about 72 per cent for men. In women, it’s 77 per cent. articles.title_orig: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a 'gift to Putin'
articles.title_zh: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a 'gift to Putin'
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies.
Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine.
Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.
Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".
"We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.
He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small".
He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US".
"Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms."
The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.
The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.
The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace.
"We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace."
Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.
Putin said he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Its diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, according to International Energy Agency estimates.
Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.
But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying they were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, and the details of exactly how Russia will supply this fuel to the global market is unclear.
But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.
With the looming US elections - which will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.
Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.
Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.
